title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). Two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions) and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. Because the same shared candidate was delivered to both conditions and the identical deterministic validator performed runtime acceptance and post‑hoc scoring, the preregistered paired difference estimand was effectively untestable in this execution. The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt‑5‑mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime guard and scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics. Confirmatory outcomes (archived artifacts) show complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). We present the preregistered methodology, the exact artifact‑grounded results, an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why the design choices produced a ceiling, and concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden future benchmarks so they expose generator×guard interactions.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into network configuration artifacts and staged change workflows (canaries, progressive rollout, rollback). Prior work shows LLMs can produce syntactically plausible configuration templates in controlled settings while separate research demonstrates verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops and deterministic network verifiers reduce syntactic and semantic errors in IaC and related domains. The operational safety question for agentic NetOps pipelines is end‑to‑end: how do generator variability, runtime verification, staged rollout semantics, repair, and rollback interact to affect safe‑deploy outcomes? Research question. Under the benchmark semantics used here, does integrating a deterministic runtime validator with an LLM generator increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) measured on N=400 preregistered paired tasks. Contribution. We (1) executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (2) report exact, archive‑verifiable confirmatory results showing universal acceptance of shared generator outputs by the deterministic validator (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0); and (3) provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis demonstrating that the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics combined with reusing the same deterministic validator produced a deterministic ceiling that makes the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard interaction in this run, together with concrete artifact‑grounded benchmark‑hardening recommendations.
sections.related_work: We position the study at the intersection of intent→configuration generation, verifier‑guided IaC workflows, deterministic network verification, and agentic/tool‑augmented LLM systems. Intent→configuration research demonstrates LLM capability to synthesize configuration templates in benchmarks and testbeds (Nguyen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025), typically focusing on generation quality rather than staged‑rollout safety. Verifier‑guided workflows and verifier‑guided fine‑tuning (e.g., TerraFormer) report correctness gains in IaC and provisioning contexts but do not demonstrate production‑scale closed‑loop runtime blocking with staged rollouts (Jana et al., 2026). Deterministic verifiers and reachability tools (header‑space and Kubernetes reachability analyses) effectively find configuration errors in emulated and offline settings (Liu et al., 2025; Koc, 2026), though tool scope and modeling assumptions vary. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) extend AIOps/RCA capabilities but introduce failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and miscalibrated confidence—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployments (Pei et al., 2025; Taparia et al., 2026). Survey and review articles highlight an evaluation gap: the absence of community‑standard, action‑aware benchmarks that combine generation, runtime blocking, staged rollouts, repair, rollback, and provenance (Rahman & Swapnil, 2026; Huang et al., 2024). Our experiment operationalizes a compact action‑aware staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to directly probe verifier utility and to surface practical design pitfalls for future confirmatory studies.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimands. The study was preregistered (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). The primary confirmatory estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (two‑sided inference, α=0.05). The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) implements a permutation‑based paired difference test and reports exact permutation p‑values; an exact McNemar two‑sided test was produced for corroboration. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary outcomes. Crucial design note. The preregistration specified shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false) and used the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer; these two choices together render the preregistered paired estimand effectively untestable when the shared candidate satisfies the deterministic validator. Adapter semantics and execution. Execution used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and scorer. For each task the adapter requested a single shared candidate from gpt‑5‑mini, delivered that candidate identically to both baseline and guarded episodes, and (for guarded episodes) routed the candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which applied full intent‑constraint validation using a deterministic rule set recorded in validator_trace entries. The preregistered repair policy permitted up to one repair attempt in the guarded episode; repair invocations, repair_applied flags, validation_before/after states, and final validity decisions were recorded. Deterministic replay and exclusions. Tasks were generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and annotated with structured difficulty metadata (changed_interface_count, dependency_rule_count, pattern, required_command_count, level ∈ {medium, hard, very_hard}). The preregistration required deterministic three‑replay consistency checks for each agent+simulator pair; pairs failing replay or encountering simulator errors were to be excluded per the missingness_plan. Analysis procedures. The primary analysis used exact permutation on paired safe‑deploy booleans (α=0.05) implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1. The exact McNemar test was reported for corroboration. Secondary outcomes included bootstrap CI for median time‑to‑rollback and counts of repair attempts; preregistered sensitivity analyses (treating excluded pairs as failures or restricted permutations) were specified. All analysis code, seeds, and logs are archived in analysis artifacts.
sections.results: Execution accounting and reconciliation. The run started 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation); complete_pairs = 400. Deterministic three‑replay checks passed for all pairs; no exclusions were recorded. Primary confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑grounded). The primary contingency counts were baseline_success_count = 400 (baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and guarded_success_count = 400 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n_11 = 400 with n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0, yielding observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. The preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Cohen's h = 0.0. These numbers are reproduced directly from the archived analysis artifacts. Repair and rollback observations. Across the 800 episodes repair_applied = false and no rollbacks were invoked; validator_trace entries show validation_after.final_state matched expected_final_state for accepted configurations. This explains universal acceptance: when the shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5, both episodes necessarily recorded safe‑deploy outcomes. Aggregated difficulty summary (artifact‑extracted). The benchmark’s per‑task difficulty labels are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; aggregating those labels yields the following distribution across N=400 tasks: medium = 80 (20.0%), hard = 160 (40.0%), very_hard = 160 (40.0%). This aggregated summary is computed from the archived task manifest and is reported here as a factual artifact‑derived characteristic of the run. Statistical interpretation. The observed ceiling collapses inferential variance: permutation and McNemar tests correctly report p = 1.0, but those statistics do not provide evidence about generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics because the design prevented the guard from having an opportunity to intervene. The preregistered power calculation assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and within‑pair variability sufficient to detect an absolute difference of ≈0.10 with N=400; those assumptions are invalidated by the observed deterministic ceiling and therefore the original power rationale does not apply to these results.
sections.discussion: Why the primary estimand became uninformative. Two preregistered design choices produced the deterministic ceiling. First, shared_initial_generation intentionally removed generator variance by delivering identical LLM outputs to baseline and guarded episodes. Second, the runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the deterministic validator accepts the shared candidate, both conditions record identical safe‑deploy outcomes and the paired difference must be zero. This is a construct‑validity outcome of the frozen design, not a general null statement about verifier utility across diverse generator/validator pairings. Consequences for power, inference, and interpretation. The preregistered power calculation relied on within‑pair variability that did not occur in this run. The observed ceiling thus invalidates the power rationale and collapses inferential uncertainty: exact p‑values of 1.0 correctly reflect the data but cannot adjudicate whether a runtime guard would have improved outcomes under an alternative design that preserved generator variance. Artifact‑grounded benchmark hardening recommendations. Using archived validator_trace and execution accounting we recommend concrete steps for future preregistered runs that preserve signal for generator×guard interactions: (1) independent per‑condition generation (independent_condition_generation = true) so each condition receives independently sampled generator outputs and the guard has bona fide opportunities to accept, block, or request repair; (2) distinct runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer implementations (or a held‑out scorer) to prevent conflation of runtime acceptance and analysis scoring; (3) controlled adversarial seeding: preregistered perturbation seeds guaranteed to produce nontrivial baseline failure rates to preserve power; (4) difficulty‑stratified sampling to ensure a sufficient proportion of very_hard tasks to produce measurable baseline errors (the archived task manifest already records difficulty labels enabling deterministic stratified sampling); (5) instrumented mitigation metrics: enable and record repair attempts, repairs applied, and time‑to‑rollback as preregistered secondary outcomes (these fields are present in validator_trace entries and repair logs). Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners, two practical lessons are immediate: (i) experiment designs that remove generation variance can hide the potential benefits of runtime guards; and (ii) independent adjudication channels (distinct scorers or human reviewers) are important for measuring guard impact. Benchmarks intended to validate runtime safety mechanisms should preserve signal for guard interventions by incorporating independent generation, adversarial perturbations, or heterogeneous validators.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling effect resulted from frozen design and implementation homogeneity and renders the primary estimand uninformative for generator×guard closed‑loop interactions in this run. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts to enable reproducibility and to support hardened follow‑on experiments (independent generation, adversarial seeding, heterogeneous validators) that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. The artifact‑grounded hardening recommendations supplied here offer concrete, preregisterable steps researchers can take to preserve statistical signal when evaluating runtime verifier utility in NetOps settings. Reproducibility note. All execution and analysis artifacts supporting the numbers and traces reported here are archived in the bundled artifact set (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts include the execution manifest, raw results, model configuration, deterministic validator traces, the task manifest with per‑task difficulty metadata, and the analysis results. Final interpretive boundary. The null paired difference observed here is a valid, artifact‑grounded outcome for the preregistered design. It should not be interpreted as evidence that runtime verification is unnecessary in general; rather, it illustrates how specific preregistered design choices can eliminate the statistical signal needed to evaluate generator×guard closed‑loop effects. Evaluations that wish to measure guard utility must preserve generator variance and independent adjudication as described above.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory): Declared generator: gpt‑5‑mini. Orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) as preregistered. Runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Preregistration: cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 (preregistration SHA‑256 recorded in the execution manifest). The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Topic constraints were selected pre‑lock by the Research Director and limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focused on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. Permitted tools and capabilities: hosted model API calls, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for runtime guarding and post‑hoc scoring, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. The guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically accepted or blocked candidates per the preregistered adapter policy; the adapter allowed up to one repair call per task but no repairs were applied (repair_applied = false across episodes). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). Autonomous literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting occurred post‑lock under the master prompt autonomy constraints; no human manually edited the technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: the experiment used a single generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for follow‑on preregistered work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and can be aggregated by auditors; this manuscript includes the artifact‑derived aggregated difficulty summary in Results and does not invent other aggregated statistics.
